claims.text: The precursor is a nominally equiatomic WTaVTi refractory high-entropy alloy.
The precursor has a single-BCC, directionally solidified dendrite–interdendrite structure containing about 71 vol.% W/Ta-rich dendrites and 29 vol.% connected Ti/V-rich channels.
Immersion in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h creates a bicontinuous, directionally aligned RHEA–Cu composite.
Liquid-metal dealloying selectively extracts Ti from the precursor's interdendritic channels while retaining RHEA ligaments.
The resulting composite contains approximately 63.6 vol.% BCC RHEA ligaments and 36.4 vol.% nearly pure FCC Cu channels.
A roughly 300 nm thick W-rich passivating interlayer forms spontaneously at every RHEA/Cu interface.
The dealloyed composite contains minor HCP Ti-rich precipitates.
Ti has a negative heat of mixing with Cu.
Ti preferentially dissolves during dealloying by exchanging with Cu.
W, Ta, and V remain in RHEA ligaments because they are immiscible with Cu.
Continued Ti extraction drives formation of the W-rich interfacial layer, which arrests further exchange.
Directionally aligned Cu channels provide efficient pathways for lattice-mediated thermal transport.
The aligned Cu channels substantially increase the composite's elevated-temperature thermal conductivity relative to conventional W–Cu composites.
The composite's thermal-conductivity advantage should emerge above approximately 650 °C.
Above 1000 °C, the composite should outperform conventional W–Cu composites in thermal conductivity.
At sufficiently high temperature, the composite should outperform pure tungsten in thermal conductivity.
The complex RHEA matrix enhances resistance to He-induced swelling.
The RHEA ligaments maintain the composite's mechanical durability.
Under 25 keV He+ implantation up to approximately 8–8.5 × 10^17 atoms cm−2, the composite should exhibit less swelling and blistering than pure W and conventional W–Cu composites.
Low-energy He+ screening results are not claimed to establish performance under full neutron-irradiation environments.
